analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers sell individual health plans across state lines under the rules of one state of their choice.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from July 2017 until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a health insurer pick one state — its "primary state" — and sell individual insurance policies in every other state under that state's rules alone. Insurers would be exempt from most laws of the states where their customers actually live, including rules on mandated benefits and premium restrictions, though secondary states could still police insurer finances, fraud, and unfair claims practices. Policies would have to carry a plain-language warning that they may be cheaper because they skip some of the buyer's own state's protections. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers gain the ability to choose which state's rules govern their individual policies nationwide, likely gravitating toward the state with the lightest requirements. Some buyers — mainly healthier people who want bare-bones, lower-premium coverage — could get cheaper plans. People with expensive medical needs could lose, as healthier buyers drift into lightly regulated plans and the remaining risk pools in each state get costlier.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers and buyers of bare-bones plans

how_it_helps.text: Insurers could sell into any state while being governed and enforced against only by their chosen primary state, freeing them from each secondary state's laws regulating how they operate there.

Buyers could see lower premiums because the bill's own required disclosure says a policy "may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws and regulations" of the buyer's state, including mandated services and rate-change restrictions.

The bill includes some consumer guardrails: insurers could not reclassify a policyholder or raise that person's premium based on health status at renewal, must offer independent external review of claim denials, and must use a bold printed notice warning buyers that the policy skips some of their state's protections.

Secondary states keep limited powers — they can still tax the issuer, examine its finances, require participation in insolvency guaranty funds, and enforce rules against fraud and unfair claims settlement practices.
The GAO would have to study ongoing effects on the uninsured, prices for people with pre-existing conditions, benefit reductions, and fraud, with annual reports for five years.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers who purchase these policies give up their own state's consumer protections, mandated benefits, and restrictions on rate changes, as the bill's required notice states. People who remain in — or are pushed back into — fully regulated plans could face higher premiums as healthier customers migrate to lightly regulated coverage, and a buyer's home state would have little power to enforce even the primary state's rules, since sole enforcement jurisdiction goes to the primary state.
analysis.who_pays_short: State regulators and buyers of such plans

drawbacks.text: The bill's own mandatory disclosure concedes that policies sold into a state would not be subject to that state's consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes, so a buyer's recourse depends entirely on the insurer's chosen state.

The bill cuts off most of a secondary state's authority over coverage sold to its own residents, including regulation of how the insurer operates there, leaving the state with only the narrow exceptions the bill lists (taxes, financial examinations, fraud, unfair claims practices, insolvency funds, and external review).

If healthier people shift into lightly regulated plans, the people left in each state's regulated market would be sicker on average, pushing premiums up — one of the very effects the bill orders the GAO to study.

Even under the bill, insurers must build coverage that works in distant states, and insurers historically have limited use of interstate sales because provider networks and medical costs differ by region — so the promised premium savings may be smaller than advertised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real tradeoff rather than a clear win: healthier buyers might find cheaper coverage, but the mechanism is letting an insurer escape the buyer's state rules rather than making coverage better. The strongest safeguard is the required warning label plus external appeal rights, and states keep some backstop powers over solvency and fraud. Whether the bargain pays off for the people buying the policies — and what happens to those left behind in the fully regulated market — is exactly what the bill leaves to a GAO study after the fact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended, so it never came to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Biggs introduced the bill on July 18, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No cosponsors signed on at any point during the 115th Congress.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators and the existing state-by-state regulatory system, which stayed untouched. The insurer and buyer benefits the bill promised never materialized, but neither did the erosion of state consumer protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators; the status quo held

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Greg Walden (R-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no measurable partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would let each insurer pick one state's rules to govern all its individual policies nationwide, exempting it from most regulation in every other state. That expands insurers' freedom and could mean cheaper bare-bones plans for some buyers, but it does so by weakening the consumer protections of the state where the customer lives.

Secondary states would lose most authority over policies sold to their own residents, and the primary state would have sole jurisdiction to enforce its laws — though states keep narrow powers over solvency, fraud, unfair claims practices, and guaranty funds. The bill narrows the consumer-protection role states currently play.
